carousels.name: How to recruit a recovery ally: 5 steps (84% have no one)

slides.title: 5 steps to recruit someone [[who'll help you stay off p*rn.]]
slides.sub: 84% of p*rn users say no one helps them avoid it.

slides.title: Have [[no one]]
slides.body: In a Barna / Pure Desire survey of 2,976 U.S. adults (2023), 84% of p*rn users said no one helps them avoid it. You don't have to be one of them.

slides.title: Steps [[1–2]]
items: Pick the right person — someone steady who won't joke or judge.
Choose a calm moment — in person or a call, not a rushed text.

slides.title: Steps [[3–4]]
items: Use a simple script: "I'm working on quitting p*rn. Would you check in with me once a week?"
Keep the ask small — one check-in, a few questions.

slides.title: Step [[5: start]]
items: Agree on a day and time.
Pick 3 questions they'll ask every week.
Tell them about slips within 24 hours.
Thank them — often.

items: Getting up when the alarm goes off.

carousels.name: 4 lies about 'I'll quit p*rn when I'm in a relationship' (harsh)

slides.title: 4 lies behind "I'll quit p*rn [[when I'm in a relationship."]]
"She'll [[fix]] it"
slides.body: A relationship doesn't remove the habit — it adds someone who can get hurt by it. P*rn comes with you.

slides.title: "I won't [[need]] it"
slides.body: Many men in relationships still watch p*rn — often in secret. Need isn't the issue. Habit is.

slides.title: Lies [[3–4]]
items: "It'll be easy then." Stress, distance and boredom still happen.
"I'll know when to stop." You've said that for years.

slides.title: Do it [[now]]
items: Quit for you, before anyone else is involved.
Build the habits while it's just you.
Show up whole to your next relationship.
Start today — not when you meet someone.
